evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫（Chinese University of Hong Kong）
evidence.text: The database says oracle-bone forms sometimes include 步 with 戉 as phonetic, and that the graph was first borrowed from 戉 for 歲 and later differentiated by adding dots to the 戈-shaped element; some forms instead use 步. It reports oracle-bone use for ‘year’, citing Xu Zhongshu’s proposal that one harvest season counted as a year. Later bronze forms include year/years, and later bronze variants add 月 or bamboo-slip forms add 日. These are the database’s account; it does not establish a single uncontested original graph analysis.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — oraclePiece

evidence.source: 說文解字在線查詢 / 說文解字注
evidence.text: The Shuowen entry defines 歲 as Jupiter, says it traverses the twenty-eight lunar mansions and completes a circuit in twelve months, and analyzes the graph as 从步戌聲. Duan Yucai glosses 步 as regular celestial motion and also treats 戌 as carrying phonetic and associative force. This is an early lexicographic analysis, not direct confirmation of the graph’s original formation.
evidence.title: 說文解字「歲」— Shuowen.org

evidence.text: This page reports a different account: oracle-bone forms may represent a ritual name, and it gives examples interpreted as ritual use and as ‘year’ (including 來歲); it also records disagreement over whether early form elements depict an implement, blood/dots, or 步. It cites a specific oracle-bone example ‘辛卯卜王貞、來歲、邑受年。四月’ and explains the calendrical link between Jupiter and year as an interpretation. The page’s exact source references should be consulted before treating its supplied dated corpus examples as independently verified.
evidence.kind: secondary paleographic dictionary with cited primary examples
evidence.title: 歲 — 漢字私註

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫（Chinese University of Hong Kong）
evidence.text: The database reports earliest oracle-bone forms with 戉-like shapes, later differentiated graphs, forms with 步, and subsequent bronze and Warring States variants. It describes the later small-seal graph as 从步戌聲, matching Shuowen, and notes 戉, 歲, 月 in the same Old Chinese rhyme group while 戌 belongs to a nearby group. Its account supports a proposed phonetic role for 戉 in an early form and 戌 in the transmitted seal form, but does not provide independently reconstructed readings of 戉 and 戌 on this page.

evidence.field: Middle Chinese and Old Chinese readings; definition examples

It lists modern Mandarin suì and Cantonese seoi3. The local Baxter–Sagart table row supplied in this research packet agrees with the page’s 歲 row (MC sjwejH; OC *s-qʷʰat-s); local rows are not independent external evidence. Its component 戉 reconstruction is not independently verified here, so no phonetic sound match between 戉 and 歲 is asserted beyond the cited paleographic analysis.

evidence.text: The page says simplified 岁 was adapted from the cursive form of traditional 歲, and calls 山 and 夕 shorthand shapes for 步 and 戉 respectively. The simplified form’s shape history is reported here; its modern visible subshapes should not be read as independent semantic components.

gaps: The original referent and pronunciation of the earliest 戉-like or dotted graph are not independently established here; therefore the claimed sound relationship between a named weapon/tool and the borrowed word cannot be fully tested.

CUHK’s accessible account and the other opened reference describe competing models: early graph borrowing/differentiation and ritual-use interpretations versus a movement/phonetic analysis. Primary inscription images and full corpus contexts were not inspected, so the earliest sense and precise dated attestations remain provisional.

The semantic development among ritual use, year/harvest, age, and Jupiter is not demonstrated as a continuous chronology. The Jupiter-to-year calendrical explanation is reported by lexicographic sources, but should not be treated as proof of the earliest spoken sense.

The Shuowen seal-form analysis is 步 + 戌; early-form 戉 and transmitted-form 戌 are distinct claims. No verified pronunciation/reconstruction pair for 戉 and 歲 in one reconstruction system was obtained, so no explicit sound comparison is supplied.

Official Unicode Unihan character pages for 岁, 歲, 步, 戉, and 戌 were inaccessible through the browser. The supplied local kMandarin rows confirm 岁 and 歲 as suì, but cannot substitute for external click-through evidence; component readings were not locally supplied.

The earliest graph remains disputed: CUHK reports both early borrowing/differentiation from 戉 and variants analyzed with semantic 步 plus phonetic 戉; Shuowen later analyzes the seal graph as 步 + 戌. Primary inscription images and full contexts were not inspected, so a single original formation cannot be selected confidently.

The depicted weapon’s spoken name and pronunciation are not independently established here. A reconstruction for 歲 alone cannot establish the weapon-name-to-year-word sound match. The compound phonetic claim 戉 remains a source analysis without an independently checked paired reconstruction in one system.

The early sense trajectory is not continuous: ‘year’ examples and a harvest-season explanation are source-reported; Shuowen’s Jupiter definition and later year/age/harvest glosses do not by themselves establish the chronological semantic path. The dates of cited bronze artifacts and Juyan slips were not established from primary records in this pass.

The official per-character Unihan pages for 岁, 歲, 步, and 戉 remained inaccessible. Local readings were checked as supplied, but only 歲 has a supplied Baxter–Sagart row; no phonetic comparison is claimed.
Dong Chinese and Wiktionary were opened/reviewed but not used as primary support for the simplified-form lineage. The proposed cursive derivation of 岁 is not independently confirmed here.

The Commons image is a modern vector redraw. No ancient artifact photograph or securely sourced Xiaoxuetang glyph was selected. Bulk reuse of recurring database material was not evaluated or recommended; the single Commons file is public domain according to its exact file page.

Oracle-bone ‘year’ and ritual uses remain reports from paleographic sources; primary inscription images and full contexts were not inspected, and the individual artifacts are not absolutely dated here.

The historical path among ritual uses, year/harvest, age, and Jupiter is not demonstrated as a continuous chronology. The Jupiter-to-year explanation is a lexicographic interpretation, not proof of the earliest spoken sense.

For the seal-script component account, Shuowen explicitly labels 戌 as phonetic, but the local Baxter–Sagart readings differ substantially between 戌 (*s.mi[t]) and 歲 (*s-qʷʰat-s). Treat that as a transmitted source analysis, not an independently established historical sound match. The nearby Old Chinese group classification reported by CUHK is not itself a reconstructed pronunciation comparison.

For early 戉, the local Baxter–Sagart values (*[ɢ]ʷat and *s-qʷʰat-s) show a closer comparison, but the weapon’s original spoken name is not independently established. The proposed borrowing may concern the graph rather than a recoverable weapon-name-to-word sound transfer.
The per-character official Unihan pages for 岁, 歲, 步, 戉, and 戌 were inaccessible. Their exact local kMandarin rows were checked but cannot serve as external click-through citations.

The official Baxter–Sagart PDF was surfaced by search but returned 502 on open. The local table rows were checked and preserve the dataset notation; no external page was successfully inspected for those rows.
The oracle-bone and bronze examples are reported by CUHK, but primary inscriptions and their full contexts were not inspected here; the earliest sense and precise dates remain unresolved.

Early graphic accounts conflict: CUHK reports both a 步-plus-戉 analysis and borrowing/differentiation from 戉. The transmitted seal analysis 步 plus 戌 is a later lexicographic account, not proof of the graph’s original formation.

The depicted weapon’s ancient spoken name is not established in the inspected sources. A proposed phonetic role for 戉 therefore does not by itself demonstrate a weapon-name-to-year-word sound borrowing.
No verified source here establishes a continuous semantic chronology among ritual use, year/harvest, age, and Jupiter. The Jupiter-to-year explanation is a reported calendrical interpretation.

The local packet’s Mandarin and Baxter–Sagart rows are not external evidence. Official per-character Unihan pages and the Baxter–Sagart primary table were not successfully inspected in this invocation, so no paired historical pronunciation claim is added.
The cited simplified-form lineage from cursive 歲 to 岁 remains supported only by dossier material in this task; it was not independently reverified in this web pass.

Bulk reuse of CUHK material is not recommended: its reuse terms for repeated database extracts were not verified. The selected Commons glyph is a single public-domain modern redraw, not evidence for an ancient artifact image.
